context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
A small parcel of 3 or 4 tendrilliferous plants go to you today. I wish there were more— with them is a flowering plant of the Lagerstrœmia with its 2 forms of stamen—

All are tropical except the Cissus antarctica— They go by Rail today & will no doubt arrive at Bromley tomorrow (Saturday).

I hoped to have gone to Down on tomorrow night for Sunday, but Boott is very ill, & must go & see him— he is I hope better but in a very hazardous state—the lungs again.

When I go to you may I bring Willy with me? he will be no plague to any one & can amuse himself now.

You will find a paper on Tendrils of Cucurbit. in Ann. Sc. Nat. by Naudin who I think proves them to be foliar in the opinion of most readers, but I have no opinion of my own

Have you seen Decaisne on Pear vars.?—no great novelty but authoritative, & hence useful.— He says that Larkspurs’ fertilize before Expansion—

Wollaston was here the other day & spent 2 days very pleasant, looking dreadfully ill. he snubs Bates & all that kind of work (yours of course included) consumedly—like a good thoroughly consistent out & out uncompromising species-monger & typic of an Entomologist.

Oliver goes to country tomorrow   my Father is away & I am “Head-clerk, Cook & bottle-washer” to the Establishment.

I cannot get to Down for at least 3 weeks I fear.

Examinations come thick & fast for first 3 weeks of August

The plants arrived on Saturday. The whole lot (far more than 3 or 4) are really priceless treasures; I hardly know which I am most curious about. It is very odd that gardeners shd. not have noticed the movement of the shoots of simple climbing plants. The Apocyneæ, which you gave me go on swinging great shoots, 18 inches long, round & round day & night. What a curious rhythmical contraction or expansion there must be; for there is no twisting of the shoot. The common garden pea, both shoot & tendrils are in constant movement. What a mistake the old one was that animals moved & plants did not.— I long to look at pollen of Lagerstrœmia; I have just finished crossing, marking &c &c &c. 134 flowers of Lythrum; so I will work out that case well, with the 96 crosses made last year.

How desperately hard worked you must now be. Do not come here till you can do it with smooth conscience & by all means bring Willy. It is, however, probable we may be away for about a fortnight towards end of this month.— I shall so like to see you.—

I am very sorry to hear about kind-heart Dr. Boott.

I fear I am an incubus to you; for I enclose 3 questions, which at any time I shd. be grateful for answer—

Ever yours affecty.— | C. Darwin

Reference to Decaisne on Pear-trees: is in it that he mentions Larkspurs?

I have “Henslow’s Botany”;—“Asa Gray’s Lessons.”; “Aug. St. Hilaires Leçons de Botanique”: can you name any good book with miscellaneous information for me to get. Did not Henfrey translate some German Book on Bot. Phys.—

I have had lots of letters on Catasetum tridentatum seeding: I have good reason to suspect there are two species under this name. Hence it wd. be important for me to examine same plant that I had before. Can you lend me a plant? or is this too unreasonable? I wish to try to fertilise it.—
